item.title: Trump’s Tariffs Force Some Canadian Companies to Consider Moving South
item.description:
At Northern Cable, the machinery that churns out steel-clad cable runs 24 hours a day, seven days a week. The push isn’t driven by a flood of new orders. It’s driven by fear.

The Canadian company is rushing to fill warehouses across the United States. It is one of many businesses making goods in Canada for U.S. customers that now face pressure to move their factories south of the border to avoid President Trump’s 50 percent tariffs, which are scheduled to start next week, on their products.

Mr. Trump’s latest tariff salvo hits particularly close to home for Northern Cable. Its factory, partly housed in a former Coca-Cola bottling plant, sits about 2.5 miles north of the invisible line dividing Ontario and New York State along the St. Lawrence River.

With half of its business coming from the United States, the company is now considering a move south. It would be a striking reversal for Northern Cable, which was founded in 1996 to keep cable-making in Brockville, Ontario, after a U.S.-based company closed its plant there and shifted production out of Canada.

But if Mr. Trump’s tariffs on a wide range of goods, including electric cable, take effect as planned on Aug. 19, Shelley Bacon, the company’s chief executive, said that he and Todd Stafford, its president, will have to start looking for an American factory.

“Todd and I are going to have to to go down and go shopping,” Mr. Bacon said, seated at a boardroom table where short lengths of cable made at the factory were displayed under glass. “We have too many jobs at stake here to just do nothing.”

Northern Cable normally divides production of its armored electrical cables — which power everything from office towers to underground mines — evenly between Canadian and American customers. But to stock its U.S. warehouses, about 80 percent of the cable now being wound onto spools that weigh up to 12,000 pounds is being made to American electrical standards. Mr. Stafford estimates that the U.S. warehouses will be emptied within two to three weeks.

Northern Cable, which has 320 employees, is not alone. A survey of 275 manufacturers conducted by the polling firm Angus Reid for KPMG found that 29 percent had moved some or all of their production to the United States since Mr. Trump started his trade war with Canada. Another 13 percent more were considering it. (The survey was conducted in May before Mr. Trump announced his latest 50 percent tariffs.)

“If the trade and tariff uncertainty continues and if there is not a focus from the government on some of the systemic issues that impact manufacturing in Canada, these manufacturers may not have a choice but to start moving to the U.S.,” said Anamika Gadia, KPMG’s national leader for industrial markets in Canada. “It’s not necessarily their desire. But they may be left with little choice.”

In Ottawa, Ambico makes highly specialized doors — bullet-resistant, blast-resistant, soundproof, fireproof and eavesdropping-proof — found in buildings, including the Pentagon and the Eisenhower Executive Office Building at the White House complex. Jack Shiner, the company’s chief executive, once had no idea where the steel arriving at his factory was made; it simply came flattened and roughly cut from a processor in Montreal.

But after the United States imposed a 25 percent tariff on products made largely from steel or aluminum, Mr. Shiner made sure that the supplier sent only U.S.-made steel, cutting the effective tariff rate on the company’s doors, which cost roughly $5,000 to $20,000 each, to about 10 percent.

“So I’m not going to be susceptible for the moment,” Mr. Shiner said. “The problem is what happens when the administration changes its mind tomorrow afternoon or next month or in three months? Nobody knows.”

Ambico, started by Mr. Shiner’s father and uncle in 1955, initially only sold metal doors and frames around Ottawa before expanding into Montreal and Toronto. After Mr. Shiner returned in 1980 from university and theological studies in the U.S., he pushed to expand into upstate New York. It was an unconventional idea at the time for a small Canadian manufacturer outside the auto industry, years before Canada and the United States signed their first free-trade agreement in 1989.

“I had this comfort with doing business in America, just 45 minutes from here, ” Mr. Shiner said. “Then we realized that there was a lot more business in the upper-tier states than there was in Ontario and Quebec — and there wasn’t the competition.”

About two-thirds of Ambico’s business now comes from the United States. Still, Mr. Shiner said, he will not move the company south.

“The 120 people that I employ here know that I’m not,” he said. “But how am I going to sustain my business is really the question.”

A few years ago, Ambico explored opening a second plant in upstate New York but abandoned the idea after concluding it could not find enough workers. Instead, Mr. Shiner plans to license some of the company’s technology to American door makers and expand into Europe, where Ambico is now certifying its doors for European standards. He expects that market to replace only about 15 percent of the company’s business.

He said that he expects the company may lose money for one or two years because of the tariffs. “I think we can weather the storms,” he said. “I do. Maybe I’m being naïve.”

Northern Cable is also eyeing Europe, though the path is harder. European electrical standards do not currently allow armored electrical cable to be used as industrial wiring, so cables must be threaded through steel pipes instead. Mr. Stafford said the company is seeking approval to change that, but expects the process could take 15 years.

Mr. Trump is not Northern Cable’s only trade headache. Mr. Bacon said that after the United States imposed steep tariffs on electrical cables from China, those products began flowing into Canada.

China exported about 538 million Canadian dollars worth of wire and cables to Canada in 2024, up from 327 million dollars in 2015. (In 2024 Canada imported 872 million dollars in cables from the United States and shipped cables worth 704 million dollars to American customers.)

“We’re getting hammered at in Canada by Chinese imports,” Mr. Bacon said, adding that he’s frustrated by what he views as a lack of interest in the Canadian government about the situation, although Canada recently imposed tariffs on some smaller cables from China, a minor product in Northern Cable’s portfolio.

Like Mr. Shiner, Mr. Stafford said he was worried about finding enough workers for an American plant that would not entirely escape tariffs. Canadian companies would still need to import large amounts of aluminum because the United States has limited capacity to produce the metal. Right now that aluminum faces a 50 percent tariff.

But if new Trump tariffs take effect on Aug. 19, Mr. Stafford said the company will move quickly.

“We’re going to have to go into overdrive to figure out: Where can we get some space, where can we put some machines? How can we start this process?” he said. ”We’ve started now, but just quietly right now.”

item.title: They Spoke English, Wore U.S. Flags and Attacked Fishermen. Who Were They?
item.description:
Far out in the Pacific Ocean, Ecuadorean fishermen have been attacked by unidentified “gringos” using drones, survivors say, spurring a mystery over whether the American military, the armed forces of another country or private military contractors were behind the strikes.

One fishing boat has been lost at sea since January, the U.N. says, with eight people still missing and presumed dead. The survivors of two other vessels said they came under attack in March by English-speaking assailants wearing matching uniforms with American flag patches, but without any clear insignia to link them to an official government force.

Some of the surviving fishermen said they had been hauled out of the water, questioned and then handed over to El Salvador’s navy before being released. The Pentagon has denied involvement, as has the U.S. Coast Guard.

Survivors have also said that a plane followed and seemingly surveilled them before the strikes.

The New York Times analyzed flight data and found that a maritime patrol plane — based out of a military base in El Salvador — flew in the direction of all three boats in the days before they were attacked. The pilots onboard spoke English with American accents, according to air traffic control communication recordings.

And as the boats moved through the ocean, the plane’s course also shifted to remain pointed at each of them over several days, The Times analysis found. Flight tracking data shows that the plane flew toward the boat that went missing in January, the Fiorella, on four different days, including on the day it disappeared.

Last transmission on Jan. 20

Left port onJan. 13

Sources: National Directorate of Aquatic Spaces of the Ecuadorian Navy, Flightradar24, Juan Alvia.

Daniel Wood/The New York Times

But the plane does not appear on the Pentagon’s lists of active aircraft. Instead, it was registered last October to a company that lists its address as a private mailbox in a UPS store in Richmond, Va., according to Federal Aviation Administration records.

Since the Pentagon started blowing up boats in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean last September, accusing them of being used for drug trafficking, dozens of vessels have been attacked, killing at least 221 people.

Washington has not been shy about claiming the strikes, often publishing footage on social media of tiny fishing boats cutting through the water before being obliterated by American munitions.

These attacks, however, have gone unclaimed.

It is certainly possible that the U.S. or some other military has conducted clandestine attacks on boats in the region. But the many lingering questions surrounding the fishing boat attacks have led some experts to wonder whether a private military contractor has been hired by the U.S. government or one of its Latin American allies — possibly El Salvador, where the plane has operated.

“It would be one thing if the U.S. didn’t have an overt maritime strike campaign, but they do, and they’re posting snuff films of boats going up in flames regularly. And that’s what makes this even more squirrelly,” said Brian Finucane, a former State Department lawyer who specializes in the laws of war. He worked in the Obama and Biden administrations, as well as in the first Trump one.

“Who are these people that are operating, and under what authority?” Mr. Finucane asked. “And they are using a UPS store as their company address? Come on.”

Ecuadorean and Salvadoran officials did not respond to requests for comment.

In November, the plane that tracked the courses of the fishing boats was flown from Tennessee to El Salvador and stationed on the military side of an airport there, flight data show. During that time, the Pentagon began increasing its air assets at another nearby airport in El Salvador to support its counternarcotics campaign in Latin America.

Air traffic controllers told the patrol plane to park at the “military apron.” A satellite image from January shows the plane parked near military aircraft, hundreds of yards away from the closest civilian craft, and images taken from the ground show that the plane’s tail is adorned with the flag of El Salvador. Still, it is unclear what role, if any, the plane played in the attacks on the fishing boats.

The Trump administration has made Latin America one of its top foreign policy priorities, to try to stem the flow of migrants and the region’s drug cartels.

Some private military contractors have shifted in kind.

Earlier this year, the Trump administration discussed issuing “letters of marque,” which were used by the U.S. government during the 18th century, before the nation had built up its navy. The letters would allow the U.S. government to contract private security forces with maritime capabilities to protect Washington’s interests at sea and to detain vessel crews.

The letters, according to three people with knowledge of the discussions, were circulated among various agencies for their input in May and were supposed to complement the Pentagon’s boat strike campaign in the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea.

Discussions around letters of marque seemed to stall around June, and the Pentagon would not say whether any have been issued. When asked about the attacks on the fishing boats, it said, “We have no knowledge of, nor were U.S. Southern Command forces involved in, the incidents described.”

Private military contractors have been active in the hemisphere. Erik Prince, whose firm Blackwater was a notorious private military contractor hired by the U.S. government in Iraq, began touring Latin America in the lead-up to the 2024 election. Mr. Prince has met with the leaders of El Salvador and Ecuador to discuss regional security, although details of those conversations are unknown.

One of Mr. Prince’s security firms was contracted by the Haitian government last year to fight the gangs, a deal the State Department authorized. As part of that contract, Mr. Prince’s company offered maritime services to patrol Haiti’s coast, according to an official in Haiti familiar with the contract.

A spokesperson for Mr. Prince said that “neither Erik Prince nor any entities affiliated with him have any relation to these events” involving Ecuadorean fishing boats.

While the Pentagon’s strikes use sophisticated equipment, including attack planes and MQ-9 Reaper drones, the attacks on the Ecuadorean fishing vessels have been carried out by rudimentary drones fitted with explosives and deployed from a vessel manned by “gringos” with American-flag patches who never identified themselves, a lawyer representing some of the fishermen said.

Ever since the Pentagon began striking boats last year, Ecuadorean fishermen say they have been scared to go out onto the water. But the crew members of the Negra Francisca Duarte II had bills to pay and mouths to feed, they said, so they set out to sea in early March.

Satisfied with their catch, they said, they headed back to the mainland, entering Ecuador’s territorial waters in mid-March. That morning they were stopped by the nation’s coast guard, inspected and then cleared for passage, according to interviews with five of the crew.

That afternoon, they said they noticed they were being followed by a blue boat on the horizon. About an hour later, drones flew toward them and then dropped explosive devices onto their ship, injuring several crewmen and engulfing their vessel in flames.

“The boys were there, hurt and scared. Some got a fire extinguisher to try to put out the fire, but there were too many flames,” the captain of the Negra Francisca, Hernán Flores, told The Times.

As the fire grew, some of the crew members dived into the ocean while others jumped into smaller boats attached to the Negra Francisca. They headed toward the blue ship that had been following them, hoping to be saved.

“We were really scared,” Mr. Flores said.

As they approached the blue vessel, the crew members onboard ordered the fishermen to raise their hands, communicating through a translator, the fishermen said. They said they were then bound, hooded and held on deck overnight, receiving no medical attention even though some were badly injured, with open, bleeding wounds.

The men, who were armed, questioned the fishermen, asking whether they were carrying anything illegal. When an injured fisherman replied that they had been inspected by the Ecuadorean Coast Guard shortly before the attack, the men began arguing among each other, seemingly worried, the fishermen said.

The next morning, the fishermen said, they were transferred to the Salvadoran Coast Guard and taken to a naval base in La Unión, in El Salvador, where they were treated well. The Salvadoran authorities told them that when they received the Ecuadorean crew, the armed men described their captives only as shipwrecked fishermen. They were then released to the capital, San Salvador, with no charges, the crew members said.

What struck Mr. Flores was his inability to identify the group of men on the blue boat, he said. For decades, he said, he had interacted with the navies and coast guards of Ecuador, the United States and other nations that patrol the waters around Ecuador, one of the world’s biggest routes for the illicit cocaine trade. They often sailed boats that clearly identified what branch of government they belonged to — like the Navy or the Coast Guard — and wore uniforms with insignia to match, the fishermen said.

But these men wore just the American flag patches, and their vessel did not fly a flag or have other markings on it, the fishermen’s lawyer said.

A U.S. Coast Guard spokesperson said in a statement that the Coast Guard cutter Bertholf, participated in a search for the Negra Francisca, as it was only about 70 miles from the fishermen. It said it had found debris from the boat but no survivors and suspended the search after 12 hours. The Coast Guard and Pentagon denied any knowledge or involvement in the attack.

While it remains unclear who carried out the strikes, they came as the Pentagon stepped up its cooperation with allies across Latin America to combat the drug trade. In May, the Pentagon applied pressure on Guatemala to agree to joint U.S. airstrikes and other military action inside its borders, to target suspected drug groups. Ecuador agreed to a similar deal earlier this year.

Last week, U.S. Southern Command announced Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere, setting up the infrastructure for the more ambitious, Latin American-wide expansion of its war against drugs in cooperation with regional allies.

The attacks on the Ecuadorean fishermen should be a wake-up call for Latin American governments, argued Juanita Goebertus, who leads the Americas division at Human Rights Watch, which published its own report on the strikes.

“The U.S. government is prioritizing operations based on weak intelligence and with illegal use of force,” she said.

Eric Schmitt contributed reporting from Washington, and Gabriel Labrador from Mexico City. Map by Daniel Wood.

item.title: How Nigel Farage Ended Up Running Against a Man Dressed as a Trash Can
item.description:
Count Binface, a man in a trash can costume, was trying to explain why he would be a winner no matter what happened on Thursday in the most high-profile election he’s ever fought.

“Shall we do a little flowchart?” he asked me, gesturing with his gloved fingers.

If you haven’t been following British politics, you may be wondering why I was interviewing someone who claims to be an intergalactic space warrior from the planet Sigma IX. Count Binface is a character played by the writer and comedian Jon Harvey, 46, and he has run in several elections as part of Britain’s long tradition of novelty political candidates.

Now he is heading for his biggest gig yet. He is the main opposition to Nigel Farage, the leader of the right-wing populist party Reform U.K., in a special parliamentary election in Clacton, an area on England’s eastern coast.

Mr. Farage is expected to win by a landslide — he held the seat with a large majority until he resigned last month to force this vote. One recent poll suggested he could get 73 percent. But though he has sought to frame this as a “people versus the establishment” election, all of the other major political parties have refused to take part. They called it a political stunt to distract from a parliamentary investigation into a gift of five million pounds (about $6.7 million) that Mr. Farage had failed to disclose.

Count Binface, who would only be interviewed in character, is Mr. Farage’s most prominent rival in the election, although 32 other candidates are running. Some are longtime Clacton residents, such as Nick Pelas, who has lived in Clacton-on-Sea for over a decade, while three represent the Official Monster Raving Loony Party, a group once associated with Britain’s most famous novelty candidate.

If Mr. Farage “wins even with an increased majority,” Count Binface argued as he laid out his metaphorical flowchart, “but it is against 33 candidates including an alien shaped like a trash can, who’s won?”

Mr. Farage would of course disagree. Reform U.K. did not respond to requests for comment for this article, but previously, Zia Yusuf, a senior party official, told the BBC that the other parties were boycotting the vote because they were “running scared” of Mr. Farage.

Count Binface’s moment in the national spotlight began last month, when Mr. Farage, who won the seat in Clacton at the 2024 general election, announced a surprise resignation. For weeks, Mr. Farage had been under pressure after revelations over his finances, including £5 million he received from a Thailand-based cryptocurrency billionaire. A parliamentary investigation had begun into whether Mr. Farage should have declared the gift, which he received in the months before the 2024 election.

Mr. Farage resigned on July 7, before the investigation was complete, and said he would immediately run for the same seat, in an apparent attempt to reclaim the political narrative.

“Let me be absolutely clear: I have done nothing wrong,” he said, adding: “I have decided that the people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions.”

If Mr. Farage were found to have broken the rules, he could be suspended from Parliament and potentially forced to fight a second special election. All the other major parties said they would wait for the investigation to conclude, with the Conservatives saying they would contest any resulting election.

That left Count Binface, in his silvered helmet and cape, to face the Reform leader this time.

“The so-called mainstream parties have elected not to take part,” Count Binface told me. “Either because they’re terrified by my magnificence,” or because “this is all actually a bit of a sideshow.”

Any British, Irish or eligible Commonwealth citizen over 18 can run in a parliamentary election in Britain, provided they pay a £500 deposit and get the nominations of 10 people living in the area.

Over the years, British politicians have routinely shared the stage with novelty candidates in funny costumes, from Elmo to representatives of the Raving Loonies.

In Britain, said Ian Hislop, the editor of Private Eye, a British satirical magazine, it has long been understood that “it is as important to laugh at politicians as it is to vote for them.”

Count Binface challenged the former Conservative prime minister Rishi Sunak. He ran against a previous prime minister, Theresa May, too, in a previous incarnation as Lord Buckethead, which he had to abandon over a copyright dispute. He ran in London’s mayoral election against Mayor Sadiq Khan. Earlier this summer, he ran in the Makerfield special election against the Labour candidate Andy Burnham. Mr. Burnham, now Britain’s prime minister, won with 54.8 percent, while Count Binface got 0.2 percent.

Mr. Harvey, the human underneath the costume, attended the University of Oxford, where he studied classics. (In a recent appearance on the podcast “The Rest Is Politics,” he let loose a stunning flow of Ancient Greek.) He has also worked on British satirical programs as a comedy writer, including for Armando Iannucci, the creator of “Veep.”

As Count Binface, his usual campaign promises include building “at least one affordable house” — a jibe at the house-building promises of consecutive British governments, which never seem to be met. He also has a longstanding promise to nationalize Adele, and to “cut your taxes and raise everyone else’s.”

There’s a serious message underneath, about the absurdity of modern politics and the impossibility of trying to please all voters everywhere.

Clacton, a parliamentary seat centered around a faded seaside town, voted by a large margin for Brexit, Mr. Farage’s signature cause before the 2016 referendum. Mr. Farage has built a populist movement by railing against immigration and more recently promising a Trump-style program of mass deportations.

In 2024, Mr. Farage won the seat with 46 percent of the vote, while a Conservative came in second place. “This is Farage country,” said Keiran Pedley, the director of politics at the polling firm Ipsos.

Some voters in Clacton have expressed frustration at the focus on the current election’s two most notable candidates. Brian Porter, a gardener who has lived in the area for about a year, said he wanted to vote for someone local who understood the needs of the community. “You’ve got all these jokers,” he said, pointing to both Count Binface (“farcical”) and Mr. Farage, who he said was “using the election to actually hide his sins.”

“It’s becoming a laughing joke,” he added. “And it’s not. This is people’s lives. It’s our future.”

Count Binface’s strongest previous result was 1 percent in the 2021 London mayoral election. A striking success for him here would be to exceed 5 percent, at which point his £500 election deposit would be refunded.

Count Binface has spent time in Clacton campaigning, meeting residents and recording videos. He also released a more detailed list of campaign promises, including some Farage-specific ones. Lawmakers who resign midterm should be barred from the resulting special election, he said. He promised to “spend more time in Clacton-on-Sea than in Washington D.C.,” a nod to Mr. Farage’s friendship with President Trump. And he pledged to “not accept £5 million gifts from crypto billionaires (on Earth).”

Even if Mr. Farage wins on Thursday, as expected, he will have to face the outcome of the investigation into that gift.

Count Binface accepts that at that point, the media interest in his story is likely to die down. He admitted that it had delighted him: “This has been the biggest feeding frenzy for old Binny so far.” He was also keen to emphasize his regard for the democratic process, and for voters who decide to support Mr. Farage.

“He has a pitch which is very powerful to a certain part of the electorate,” he said. “We mustn’t disrespect that. If humans choose to vote for Nigel, that is democracy.”

But with the major parties absent, “I seem to be his majesty’s opposition,” he said, from behind his bin. “Which is fine.”

item.title: In Bali, a Quest to Restore the Sacred Glow of Fireflies
item.description:
Nearly a decade ago, I Wayan Wardika went back home to Bali on a vacation and found that his village was unrecognizable. Trash choked the river. Synthetic pesticides saturated the rice paddies. And the nights, once alive with the glow of fireflies, had fallen dark.

For generations, the soft glow of the lightning bugs was part of the steady rhythm of nightfall in rural Bali. Today, they are fading, driven away by climate change, aggressive land development for tourism, chemical-intensive farming and artificial light that disrupts their mating rituals.

“We used to have thousands of them illuminating the darkness,” said Mr. Wardika, who grew up in the 1990s, before his village had electricity. “The thought of future generations growing up without experiencing the magic of fireflies, as I did, breaks my heart.”

In Balinese culture, fireflies embody the Tri Hita Karana — the sacred philosophy in which humanity, nature and the divine exist in harmony. This reverence is deeply rooted in local beliefs that these glowing creatures serve as sacred messengers, a connection between living communities and their ancestors.

“They are believed to carry the spirits of ancestors and can guide lost souls,” Mr. Wardika said, explaining that fireflies are considered to be the fingernails of forebears. “My grandmother always scolded me when I caught them and put them in a jar.”

Yet beyond their spiritual charm, these glowing beetles serve as vital ecological messengers. Fireflies typically thrive in pristine, chemical-free environments. Their delicate bodies are acutely sensitive to environmental changes. Their flickering presence signals clean water, healthy soil and minimal light pollution.

Tourism has transformed much of Bali, which is part of Indonesia and where fireflies are no longer as common as they once were.

In 2018, after more than a decade of working as a server on cruise ships, Mr. Wardika moved back to Taro, an ancient village about 20 kilometers, or around 12 miles, north of Ubud, Bali. Converting a corner of his family compound he then founded the Firefly Conservation House, Indonesia’s first firefly conservation facility, which melds Balinese tradition with rigorous science.

A team of biologists at the lab conducts research ranging from field mapping and population counts to controlled rearing and breeding. Researchers build small glass terrariums they call honeymoon suites, a microhabitat designed specifically for courtship. Inside they pair lab-reared females with males caught from the wild, which they say ensures optimal breeding results.

The payoff is not quick. While an adult firefly lives for a brief 22 days, growing one from an egg into a mature beetle takes anywhere from six months to nearly two years, depending on the species.

Day by day, the researchers meticulously track every stage of the beetles’ life cycle from mating and egg-laying through the fragile larval stage. Once mating is complete or the female beetle has reached the end of its natural life, eggs are collected and placed in an incubator to hatch. The terrariums are then sanitized and prepared with soil, for terrestrial species, or water, for the semiaquatic kind, laying the groundwork for the next generation to light up the village night.

The larvae are then isolated — semiaquatic ones in petri dishes and terrestrial ones in individual glass jars. As she often does, Riris Widiari, a biologist, set out to feed row upon row of jars, equipped with a plastic container of chopped fermented worms and a pair of tweezers. Carefully, she lifted the wire mesh off the first container, placed a worm near a larva, secured the mesh and moved to the next.

Ms. Riris, who grew up in a housing complex in Bali, said she had no memory of seeing a firefly as a child. “Now, I am surrounded by them. At the moment, we have more than 1,700 jars,” she said, “and because we leave the lab dark as night falls, the larvae’s teeny glow is noticeable.”

According to the International Union for Conservation of Nature, about a tenth of all assessed firefly species are threatened. Several native Southeast Asian species have been categorized as vulnerable, and a handful are facing extinction. Researchers warn that the true figure of threatened species is likely to be much higher, as there is not enough data on more than half of all firefly species.

In Taro, Mr. Wardika’s group has brought back thousands of larvae into the surrounding controlled area. It has also identified eight native species of firefly.

“It took a lot of trial and error, and many tears to get here,” said Cindy Chayani Mangampang, one of the biologists. “None of us had any idea how to breed fireflies, and there were no local studies to follow.”

Raising fireflies inside the lab is half the battle. To ensure the fireflies have a safe environment to return to, Mr. Wardika encourages local farmers to switch to regenerative organic agriculture. To cut down on chemical use, Mr. Wardika has given out homemade compost, fruit-fermented fertilizer and natural tobacco-based pesticides.

So far, four farms have made the switch. Mr. Wardika’s goal is to enlist 35 farmers across more than 65 acres, creating a two-kilometer, or about 1.2-mile, radius of the lab to be free of synthetic chemicals.

The sanctuary also operates as an eco-tourism destination, which acts as a source of revenue.

On a recent Thursday afternoon, the bustling atmosphere at the center showcased its vital research and education work. Surrounded by floor-to-ceiling shelves stacked with glass jars of larvae, in one corner, Ms. Cindy assisted an intern in harvesting firefly eggs and carefully transferring them to new containers.

A group of tourists gathered around a worktable and listened intently to Ms. Riris’s talk about the firefly’s life cycle, observed different specimens and even used magnifying glasses to search for tiny larvae hidden beneath the leaves of water lettuce.

As darkness fell, excited oohs and ahhs broke out in hushed tones as tiny lights flickered on the ground or occasionally flew deep into the night. Some guests were given glass jars with adult fireflies, which they could release outdoors.

“Fireflies give us the wisdom,” Mr. Wardika said, “to control our actions without disrupting the ecosystem.”
